content.text:
**Выбор: кандидат 5.** Уверенность средняя — его отрыв от кандидатов 0, 1 и 4 небольшой. Всё посчитано в уме, без симуляции.

**Почему выбраны заказы раз в 2 дня.**
- **Кандидат 2 (заказ каждый день):** около 27 дней с заказом. Это примерно на 13 × 52 ≈ 676 больше фиксированных платежей, чем у планов с заказом раз в 2 дня. Экономия на хранении от меньшего запаса — примерно 300. Плата за заказы её перевешивает.
- **Кандидаты 3 и 7 (раз в 3 дня):** одна поставка — около 80–100 ед. одного товара. Плюс текущий запас второго товара и остатки — получается 150–170 ед. при вместимости 164. Есть риск, что излишек пропадёт при приходе, особенно когда спрос ниже прогноза.
- **Кандидат 6 (раз в 4 дня):** поставки по 95–132 ед. явно не помещаются на склад.
- **Кандидаты 0, 1, 4, 5 (раз в 2 дня):** поставки обоих товаров приходят по нечётным дням, вместе около 110–120 ед. плюс остатки. Это укладывается в 164.

**Объём заказов против ожидаемого спроса.** Ожидаемый спрос — прогноз за дни прихода × 1,046. Товар 0 приходит в дни 5–29, ожидаемо около 597 ед. Товар 1 приходит в дни 3–29, ожидаемо около 756 ед.

| Кандидат | Товар 0 | Товар 1 |
|---|---|---|
| 0 | 680 (+14 %) | 868 (+15 %) |
| 4 | 599 (≈ спрос) | 868 (+15 %) |
| 1 | 585 (−2 %) | 746 (−1 %) |
| 5 | 630 (+5 %) | 794 (+5 %) |

**Цена ошибки в каждую сторону.**
- **Нехватка:** товар 0 теряет 6 маржи + 5 неустойки = 11 за единицу, товар 1 — 8 + 7 = 15.
- **Излишек:** товар 0 годен 8 дней и переходит на следующие циклы, но постоянный перебор на 14 % у кандидата 0 всё равно уходит в списание: около 80 ед. × 5 плюс хранение. Товар 1 годен всего 5 дней, поэтому перебор на 15 % у кандидатов 0 и 4 — это около 110 ед. под списание по 6. Кроме того, у кандидата 0 растут остатки, и на склад давит лишний объём.
- **Заказ ровно под спрос:** у кандидата 1 при случайных колебаниях спроса (около ±30 %) будут регулярные нехватки, а они дороже излишка.

Кандидат 5 берёт запас около 5 % по обоим товарам. Это ближе всего к разумному балансу между неустойкой и списанием, и при отклонениях спроса этот план устойчивее остальных. Нехватка в первые дни (товар 0 до дня 5, товар 1 до дня 3) одинакова у всех кандидатов и на сравнение не влияет.

**Выбор: кандидат 0.** Это вывод из прикидок в уме, а не из полного пошагового расчёта, поэтому уверенность умеренная. Ниже — почему.

**Отсеянные кандидаты**
- **Кандидат 6 (заказ раз в 4 дня).** Каждая поставка покрывает около 4 дней спроса, это примерно 200 единиц и больше, а склад вмещает 164. Излишек при приходе пропадает, хотя уже оплачен. Это худший вариант.
- **Кандидаты 3 и 7 (заказ раз в 3 дня).** В день прихода на складе оказывается около 135 единиц плюс остатки, то есть почти предел вместимости. Заметная часть всплесков спроса приведёт к потере товара при приходе. Кроме того, растут хранение и списания, особенно у товара 1, который годен всего 5 дней.
- **Кандидат 2 (заказ каждый день).** Он платит фиксированные 52 примерно 27 раз против 13 у планов с заказом раз в 2 дня. Переплата около 700, а экономия на хранении примерно сопоставима. Вдобавок запас у него почти без страховки, около прогноз × 1,046, поэтому нехваток и неустоек будет больше.

**Сравнение планов с заказом раз в 2 дня (0, 1, 4, 5)**
Оба товара из таких заказов приходят в один и тот же нечётный день. В сумме это около 100 единиц плюс остатки, вместимость не нарушается.

Нужный объём заказа я оценил по формуле «газетчика»: насколько выгоднее перезаказать, чем недозаказать.
- **Товар 0.** Нехватка стоит 6 (упущенная маржа) + 5 (неустойка) = 11 за единицу. Излишек стоит не больше 5 и обычно меньше: при годности 8 дней остаток доживает до следующего цикла. Соотношение 11 к 5 даёт заказ примерно на 5 единиц выше среднего спроса за 2 дня (около 46), то есть около 51.
- **Товар 1.** Нехватка стоит 8 + 7 = 15, излишек — около 6. Это тоже даёт примерно +5 к среднему спросу за 2 дня (около 44), то есть около 49.

Как это ложится на кандидатов:

| Кандидат | Товар 0 (цель ≈ 51) | Товар 1 (цель ≈ 49) |
|---|---|---|
| 0 | 53 | 50 |
| 4 | 46 | 50 |
| 5 | 48 | 46 |
| 1 | 45 | 43 |

Ближе всех к нужному уровню кандидат 0. Он же устойчивее остальных к превышению спроса над прогнозом, а неустойки здесь дороже излишков.

I picked **Candidate 0**. I did this in my head without simulating, so the gaps between the every-2-days plans (0, 4, 5, 1) are rough estimates. Cand 3, 7, 6 and 2 fall away clearly.

**Rejected plans**
- **Every 3 or 4 days (cand 3, 7, 6).** One delivery is about 157 units in cand 3, and over 200 in cand 6. Add the stock left over and it goes past the 164 limit. The overflow is lost after it has been paid for. Product 1 is accepted second, so it is the one that gets cut, and it is also the one with the bigger shortage penalty.
- **Every day (cand 2).** That is 27 order fees of 52, about 1400 in total. A plan that orders every 2 days pays about 676. Daily orders save only about 10 per day in storage, while the extra fees cost about 26 per day.

**Choosing among the every-2-days plans (0, 1, 4, 5)**
- A missing unit costs much more than a spare one. Missing product 0 loses its margin of 6 plus the penalty of 5, so 11. Missing product 1 loses 8 plus 7, so 15. A spare unit mostly carries over to the next delivery. It costs 0.4 per day to store, and only product 1 sometimes expires (5-day shelf life).
- Demand over 2 days is about 47 units with a spread of about ±10. Because shortages cost more, the best order for product 1 is above the average, around 52–54. Cand 0 orders that, about 1.2× the forecast. Cand 1 and 5 order less.
- For product 0, cand 4 orders about 1.05× the forecast, which is roughly equal to average demand. I estimate that leads to about 4 short units per cycle, or around 500 in total. Cand 0 orders about 1.13×. Its extra stock costs roughly 250 to store, and the 8-day shelf life means it rarely expires.
- **Risk:** cand 0's stock creeps up over time, so late in the month a morning could reach about 158 of the 164 places. Overflow is possible on high-delivery days, but I think it costs less than the shortages the leaner plans would have.

Cand 5 is close behind cand 0.

I pick **candidate 5**. This is a mental estimate, not a simulation. The schedules follow clearly from the rules, but choosing among the four plans that order every two days depends on a rough newsvendor-style estimate.

**1. Ordering frequency rules out 2, 3, 6 and 7.**
- **Candidate 2** orders almost every day. That adds about 13 extra ordering fees, roughly 52 × 13 ≈ 680. The lower holding cost does not make up for that.
- **Candidates 3 and 7** order every 3 days, and **candidate 6** every 4 days. Both goods are ordered on the same day, so they arrive together. One delivery is about 150–230 units on top of what is left over, against a capacity of 164. The excess is lost but already paid for. With demand swings, candidate 6 almost certainly hits the cap and 3 and 7 probably do too, so the cap costs them money.
- **Candidates 0, 1, 4 and 5** order every 2 days. Each delivery is about 90–115 units plus leftovers, which stays within 164. The fees are moderate, so the choice is among these four.

**2. The four 2-day plans differ by how much they order above forecast.** Each delivery covers two days of forecast demand:
- Candidate 0 orders about 1.20× forecast for both goods. Candidate 1 orders about 1.02×. Candidate 4 orders about 1.05× for good 0 and 1.19× for good 1. Candidate 5 orders about 1.09–1.10× for both.
- Average demand is 1.046× forecast. Candidate 1 orders below that, so it runs short every cycle. With penalties of 5 and 7 per missing unit on top of the lost margin, it loses the most here.
- A shortage of good 0 costs about 11 per unit (margin 6 + penalty 5). For good 1 it costs about 15 (8 + 7). A unit ordered but never sold costs its purchase price, 5 or 6, plus some holding. So the target is roughly the 65–70% point of two-day demand. Before counting carry-over, that is about 1.13–1.15× forecast.
- Leftovers carry over to the next cycle: good 0 keeps for 8 days and good 1 for 5. That lowers the target a little, to roughly 1.1×.
- Candidate 0 builds a lasting surplus of about 15% that ends up written off or paying for storage. Candidate 4 gives good 0 almost no margin above average demand, so it runs short often.

Candidate 5 is closest to the best level for both goods. It is also the most robust when demand differs from forecast: it orders enough not to run short regularly, but not so much that write-offs pile up.

I pick **candidate 5**. I didn't simulate every scenario in detail. I compared the plans by fixed ordering costs, by how much they order against average demand, and by warehouse capacity.

**What goes into the comparison**
- **Shortage costs more than surplus.** A missing unit of product 0 costs 6 in lost margin plus a 5 penalty, 11 in total. A unit left over loses at most 5 plus storage. For product 1 the numbers are 15 and about 6. So it pays to order a little above the expected demand. Expected demand is the forecast × 1.046.
- **Leftovers carry over.** Unsold units stay sellable: product 0 for 8 days, product 1 for 5 days. That means a large safety stock isn't needed. Excess builds up and then gets written off, while a shortage is lost for good.

**Order frequency**
- **Candidate 2** orders every day: 27 × 52 = 1404 in fixed costs against about 676 for the every-other-day plans. The extra ~730 can't be earned back, so it's out.
- **Candidates 3 and 7** order every 3 days. They save about 208 in fixed costs, but the extra stock sitting on the shelf costs about 25 units × 0.4 × ~27 days ≈ 270 in storage. On top of that, their peaks come close to the 164-unit limit (up to about 150–163), so some arrivals would be lost. They come out slightly worse than ordering every other day.
- **Candidate 6** orders every 4 days. Its batches (120 + 102) overflow the warehouse, and the extra storage cost is even higher.

**The every-other-day plans (0, 1, 4, 5)**
Expected demand over the period when deliveries arrive is about 597 units of product 0 (days 5–29) and about 756 of product 1 (days 3–29).

| Candidate | Product 0 vs. demand | Product 1 vs. demand | Verdict |
|---|---|---|---|
| 0 | 680 ≈ 1.14× | 868 ≈ 1.15× | Too much excess: about 80 units per product get written off |
| 1 | ≈ 0.97× | ≈ 0.99× | Below demand; because a shortage is lost for good, shortfalls pile up |
| 4 | ≈ 0.99× | ≈ 1.15× | Short on product 0, too much of product 1 |
| 5 | ≈ 1.03× | ≈ 1.06× | Balanced for both |

**Robustness to random demand**
Candidate 5 holds up best when actual demand moves away from the forecast. Its small surplus covers ordinary dips, and since unsold stock stays sellable, the extra buffer is cheap to keep. It also stays well under the warehouse limit. For product 1 the gap between candidates 5 and 0 is roughly a wash per delivery: candidate 0's lower penalties are about equal to its extra write-offs. Carried-over stock tips that balance toward candidate 5. For product 0, candidate 5 is better than both candidate 0 (too much excess) and candidate 4 (too little).

**Choice: candidate 0** (moderate confidence). I did this as a rough calculation in my head and did not simulate day by day. Candidates 0 and 5 are close, so the ranking between them is the least certain part.

1. **How often to order.** Average demand is about 50 units a day for both items together. A 2-day cycle brings in roughly 110–140 units per delivery, which fits within the 164-unit warehouse limit.
   - **Ordering every 3–4 days (candidates 3, 6, 7)** brings 150–230 units at once. Add leftover stock and the limit is regularly exceeded, so the excess is lost even though it was paid for. Candidate 6 is the worst case.
   - **Ordering daily (candidate 2)** pays the 52 fee about 27 times instead of about 14, roughly 700 extra. Lower storage costs (about 150 saved) don't make up for that.
   - That leaves the 2-day plans: 0, 1, 4 and 5.

2. **How much to order.** Running short costs much more than holding a little extra:
   - Running short costs the lost margin plus the penalty: 6 + 5 = 11 per unit for item 0, and 8 + 7 = 15 for item 1.
   - An extra unit just carries over to the next cycle. Item 0 keeps 8 days and item 1 keeps 5, against a 2-day cycle, so it mostly costs about 0.8 in storage. Only steady over-ordering ends in write-offs.
   - Real demand averages about 1.046 × forecast. Over a 2-day window it varies by about 21%, which is roughly ±10 units.

3. **The four 2-day plans compared** (amounts relative to forecast demand):
   - **Candidate 1 (about 1.0×)** orders below average real demand, so it runs short regularly.
   - **Candidate 5 (about 1.07×)** has almost no buffer. I estimate about 4 units short per cycle, which is around 800 in lost margin and penalties over the month.
   - **Candidate 4** is high on item 1 but low on item 0.
   - **Candidate 0 (about 1.18×)** builds up surplus over time. It loses around 500 to write-offs and storage, mostly on item 1 because of its 5-day shelf life. In return it rarely runs short, and those shortages are the most expensive loss here.

4. **Risks for candidate 0.**
   - On day 11 about 146 units arrive at once plus about 20 left over. That could go roughly 2 units over the limit, which is a small loss.
   - It has some extra waste at the end of the month.
   - Neither changes the overall picture, and its buffer protects better than the others when demand comes in above forecast.

I'd pick **candidate 5**. It's the most balanced plan, but cand 7 runs it close: they differ by maybe a few hundred, which is within the noise of my estimates. I worked these out roughly in my head, not with a full simulation.

**The starting shortage is the same for every plan.** Product 0 has 34 units against about 125 of demand before its first delivery on day 5. Product 1 has 27 against about 60 before day 3. None of the plans can avoid this, so it doesn't separate them.

**Ordering every day (cand 2) costs too much.** That's about 27 order fees instead of 14, roughly 680 more. Smaller deliveries save only about 250–290 in storage, so cand 2 ends up around 400 behind.

**Every 4 days (cand 6) doesn't fit.** Four days of demand is about 200 units, but the warehouse holds 164. Extra units are lost on arrival and the shortages are certain.

**Every 3 days (cand 3, 7) vs every 2 days (cand 0, 1, 4, 5).** Ordering every 3 days saves about 260 in order fees but costs about 255 more in storage, so on average it's a wash. The difference is overflow risk. In cand 7, around day 12, stock is already about 158 before buffers, so with random demand some product 1 will likely be lost on arrival, just before the day-14 demand spike. Cand 3 orders even more, so its risk is higher. The every-2-day plans peak around 140 at the same point.

**How much safety stock to order.** Average demand is about 1.046 × forecast. Each plan orders a different multiple of the forecast:
- **Cand 0** orders about 1.2 × forecast for both products. That builds up about 7 extra units of each product every 2 days. Product 1 keeps only 5 days, so most of that surplus spoils or is left over at the end. I estimate about 1000 lost on product 1 alone. It also raises the overflow risk.
- **Cand 4** orders about 1.19 × forecast for product 1, with the same problem. For product 0 it orders about 1.045, which is no margin above average demand, so shortages are frequent. Each missed unit of product 0 costs 11 (lost profit plus penalty).
- **Cand 1** orders about 1.02 × forecast, below average demand. Shortages build up, and each missed unit of product 1 costs 15.
- **Cand 5** orders about 1.09 × forecast for both products. That's a small cushion: little waste, and shortages limited to the unavoidable start.

I pick **Candidate 5**. I worked this out roughly in my head rather than running a full day-by-day simulation, so treat it as a judgement call, not an exact result.

**Ordering in bigger, less frequent batches (Candidates 3, 6, 7) loses the most.**
- Candidate 6 orders every 4 days, about 200 units at a time. That is more than the 164-unit warehouse, so the extra is lost at arrival, already paid for. Product 1 also only keeps 5 days, so some of each batch spoils before it sells.
- Candidates 3 and 7 order every 3 days, about 150–190 units at a time. Together with stock already on hand, arrivals often go over 164 and the extra is lost.

**Ordering every day (Candidate 2) costs too much in order fees.** It places 27 orders against about 13 for the every-other-day plans. The extra ~14 × 52 ≈ 730 is more than it saves on storage and warehouse space.

**Among the every-other-day plans (0, 1, 4, 5), the difference is how much extra each orders over expected demand.**
- Candidate 1 orders about exactly the expected demand, already including the 1.046 average demand multiplier. It has almost no buffer, so it often runs short when demand is high. Shortages are costly: each missing unit loses its margin plus the penalty, 11 for product 0 and 15 for product 1.
- Candidate 0 orders about 17% above expected demand for both products. The surplus builds up each cycle, so stock grows. Some of product 1 spoils, and arrivals on days 11 and 13 (146 and 139 units) are close to overflowing the warehouse.
- Candidate 4 orders about 3% extra of product 0 but about 17% extra of product 1. That has the same spoilage and space problems for product 1 as Candidate 0.
- Candidate 5 orders about 6–8% extra of both products. This gives enough buffer against random demand without much spoilage or overflow. It is the best trade-off.

I'm returning −1 ("don't know"). I can rule out several plans with fair confidence, but candidates 1, 5 and 7 come out within the error of my mental estimates.

**Losses common to every plan.** The starting stock is 34 of item 0 against about 125 demand over days 0–4. For item 1 it is 27 against about 60 over days 0–2. Nothing ordered can arrive sooner, so every plan pays the same shortage penalties for these days.

**Order frequency.**
- **Daily (candidate 2):** about 13 extra order days cost about 680 in fees. Daily ordering saves only about 290 in holding, so this plan loses roughly 400.
- **Every 3 days (3, 7) vs every 2 days (0, 1, 4, 5):** the 3-day plans save 5 order days (260). They pay about the same, roughly 275, in extra holding. Item 1 arrives in bigger batches, so the warehouse is near its 164 limit, around day 12. Overall this is a draw.
- **Every 4 days (6):** an item 1 batch of 117–132 arrives while about 50 units of item 0 are still in stock. That goes over 164, and the excess is lost on arrival. This plan is the worst.

**Order size.** I compared total ordered to expected demand, using the 1.046 mean multiplier. For item 0 it is 597 units over days 5–29; for item 1 it is 756 over days 3–29.

| Candidate | Item 0 | Item 1 |
|---|---|---|
| 0 | 680 (×1.14) | 868 (×1.15) |
| 4 | 599 (×1.00) | 868 (×1.15) |
| 5 | 630 (×1.055) | 794 (×1.05) |
| 1 | 585 (×0.98) | 746 (×0.99) |
| 7 | 623 (×1.04) | 791 (×1.046) |
| 3 | 672 (×1.125) | 853 (×1.13) |

- **Candidates 0 and 4:** about 112 surplus units of item 1 pile up. Most end up written off or left over at the end, costing about 670 in purchases plus holding on a stock of 30–50. Shortages fall by only about 25–30 units. Net, these plans lose about 400 on item 1. Candidate 0 also goes over capacity around days 11 and 25.
- **Candidate 3:** the same over-ordering, plus capacity is tighter.
- **1 vs 5:** with no buffer, candidate 1 runs short by about 30–35 units per item over the month. Candidate 5's buffer of about 5% roughly halves that, which is worth about 90 per item. But the larger stock costs about 108 per item in holding. Net, they come out almost even: −18 and −13 against candidate 5. Candidate 5 is also closer to the capacity limit around day 11.
- **Candidate 7:** about the same order sizes as candidate 1, ordering every 3 days. That is also a draw.

**Uncertainty.** Shortages depend on the cumulative spread of actual demand, about ±10 units per 2-day period. The gaps between 1, 5 and 7 are a few dozen units of money, less than the error in my estimates. I can't name a single best plan with reasonable confidence, so I'm declining.

**Выбираю кандидата 5.** Уверенность умеренная: главный довод — сэкономленные 676 на оплате заказов. Учёт хранения и денег оценён грубо.

**С каким запасом заказывают планы.** Каждую партию я сравнил со спросом по прогнозу на те дни, которые она покрывает. Среднее множителя ≈ 1,046, поэтому запас примерно в 1,03 раза меньше среднего спроса.

| Кандидат | Как часто заказ | Запас к прогнозу |
|---|---|---|
| 2 | каждый день | ≈ 1,10 |
| 1 | раз в 2 дня | ≈ 1,03 (чуть ниже среднего спроса) |
| 5 | раз в 2 дня | ≈ 1,10 |
| 0 | раз в 2 дня | ≈ 1,20 |
| 4 | раз в 2 дня | товар 0 ≈ 1,05, товар 1 ≈ 1,19 |
| 3 | раз в 3 дня | ≈ 1,19 |
| 7 | раз в 3 дня | ≈ 1,10 |
| 6 | раз в 4 дня | — |

**Почему лучше брать немного больше прогноза.** Нехватка дорогая: упущенная наценка плюс неустойка — 11 за единицу товара 0 и 15 за единицу товара 1. Лишний товар стоит дёшево: он переходит на следующий день и обходится примерно в 0,4 за день хранения. Поэтому план 1 немного недозаказывает и стабильно ловит нехватку. Планы 0, 3 и товар 1 в плане 4 перезаказывают примерно на 15 %. Лишний запас копится до конца срока годности и уходит в списание, а у планов 3 и 0 ещё и упирается во вместимость склада.

**Кандидат 5 против кандидата 2.** Запас у них одинаковый, разница в частоте заказов.
- Кандидат 2 платит 52 за 27 дней с заказом, кандидат 5 — за 14. Экономия 13 × 52 = 676.
- Цена реже заказывать — лишнее хранение: примерно 280 за месяц.
- Итог: кандидат 5 впереди примерно на 400.

**Деньги в первые дни.**
- Кандидат 0 уже в день 4 не может оплатить заказ полностью: заказ урезается.
- У кандидатов 3 и 7 урезание примерно в день 3–6.
- У кандидата 6 — в день 4.
- У кандидата 5 к дню 6 остаётся примерно 30 после оплаты. Если спрос окажется ниже прогноза, часть заказа товара 1 могут урезать, но потери будут небольшими.

**Вместимость склада.** У планов с заказом раз в 2 дня партии обоих товаров приходят в один день, около 110 единиц. При умеренном остатке это помещается в 164. У планов с заказом раз в 3–4 дня (3, 6, 7) склад заполняется почти до предела или переполняется, а излишек пропадает.

**Кандидат 5 против кандидата 7.** Заказ раз в 3 дня экономит ещё примерно 260 на оплате заказов. Но лишнее хранение съедает примерно столько же, а риски по деньгам и вместимости выше. Поэтому кандидат 5 надёжнее.
